spans.assertion: tested the hypothesis that referees favor light-skinned over dark-skinned players using a dataset of 146,028 player-referee dyads from four European leagues, 2012-2013 season
controlled for player position, league country, exposure (games), height, and weight
used two-way clustered standard errors, clustered by player and by referee
primary estimand, adjusted risk difference, is 0.24 percentage points [95% CI -0.01 to 0.49], p=0.060
secondary estimand, adjusted odds ratio, is 1.21 [95% CI 1.00 to 1.46], p=0.048
overall conclusion is NOT SUPPORTED; evidence is inconclusive and does not provide sufficient support for the hypothesis
primary estimand's CI includes zero and its p-value exceeds the 0.05 threshold
the effect, even if real, is very small in absolute terms relative to a 1.2% baseline rate
risk difference point estimate is 0.2413pp, 95% CI [-0.0106, 0.4932]pp, p=0.0604, at alpha=0.05
dark-skinned players have an estimated 0.24pp higher probability of receiving a red card than light-skinned players after adjusting for confounders
the 95% CI includes zero (lower bound -0.01) and p=0.060 exceeds 0.05
cannot reject the null hypothesis of no difference at the conventional significance level
red card probability is estimated to rise from 1.21% (light) to 1.45% (dark), an absolute increase of 0.24pp
this estimate is statistically indistinguishable from zero given the uncertainty in the data
odds ratio point estimate is 1.2079, 95% CI [1.0019, 1.4561], p=0.0477
dark-skinned players have 1.21 times the odds of a red card compared to light-skinned players
the CI barely excludes 1.0 (lower bound 1.002) and p=0.048 is marginally significant
the odds ratio is significant while the risk difference is not, because the two have different standard errors from the non-linear transformation
the risk difference was specified as the primary test because it is more interpretable for rare outcomes
the inconsistency between the odds ratio and risk difference reflects the borderline nature of the evidence
unit of analysis is defined as player-referee dyads, each row covering all matches between one player and one referee
total dyads after complete case analysis is 99,645
there are 1,214 unique players in the sample
there are 2,768 unique referees in the sample
exposure group sizes are 83,655 light-skin dyads (84.0%) and 15,990 dark-skin dyads (16.0%)
there were 1,241 total red-card outcome events, a 1.25% overall rate
two independent raters coded player skin tone from profile photos on a 5-point scale from 0 (very light) to 1 (very dark)
inter-rater reliability was Pearson r=0.92 (p<0.001), indicating high agreement
the average of both raters' scores was used as the primary skin-tone measure
players were categorized as light skin (avg rating ≤0.25) or dark skin (avg rating ≥0.75)
medium skin tone (0.25<rating<0.75) was excluded from the primary analysis to create a clearer contrast
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded due to missing photos/ratings
adjusted for player position using 12 categories to control positional differences in card rates
adjusted for league country (England, France, Germany, Spain) to control country-specific refereeing standards
adjusted for exposure using log(games+1) to control for varying encounters per dyad
adjusted for player height (continuous, cm) as a proxy for physicality
adjusted for player weight (continuous, kg) as a proxy for playing style

spans.assertion: excluded 21,407 dyads missing skin tone ratings because no photo was available
excluded 17,015 dyads with medium skin tone to create a clearer contrast
excluded 7,961 dyads with missing covariates (height, weight, or position)
final analysis sample is 99,645 dyads, 68% of the original dataset
created a binary outcome (any red card vs none) from the original count variable
used log(games+1) for exposure to linearize its relationship with the outcome
used a categorical binary skin tone variable (dark vs light) for the primary analysis
the sensitivity analysis used the continuous (0-1 scale) skin tone measure instead
fit a logistic regression model for the binary outcome
used maximum likelihood as the estimation method
used the formula any_red_card ~ dark_skin + C(position) + C(leagueCountry) + log_games + height + weight
used two-way clustering at both the player and referee levels
multiple dyads per player and per referee create within-cluster correlation that violates the independence assumption
used the Cameron-Gelbach-Miller (2011) two-way clustering estimator, SE²(two-way)=SE²(player)+SE²(referee)-SE²(robust)
two-way clustering increases standard errors by ~15% versus robust SEs, making inference more conservative
used average marginal effects (AME) to convert log-odds to a risk difference
computed AME by predicting red-card probability under all-dark and all-light counterfactuals and averaging the difference across observations
computed the standard error via the delta method using the two-way clustered variance-covariance matrix
the conclusion is NOT SUPPORTED
the hypothesis is not supported by the data at alpha=0.05 for the primary estimand
primary estimand's p=0.060 exceeds alpha=0.05 and its 95% CI includes zero
effect magnitude is small: baseline (light) 1.21%, dark 1.45%, absolute increase 0.24pp, relative increase ~20% on a rare outcome
CI spans -0.01 to +0.49pp, indicating substantial uncertainty, with the true effect plausibly zero or slightly negative
conducted a power analysis
study is underpowered: minimum detectable effect at 80% power is 0.36pp, and the observed 0.24pp effect is only 67% of that threshold
subgroup analyses reveal substantial heterogeneity by country

considered alternative explanations besides bias: unmeasured confounders, reverse causality, and ecological confounding

effect appears larger at moderate exposure (2-10 games) and attenuates at very high exposure, possibly reflecting referee learning or a statistical artifact

the hypothesis is not supported by this analysis, though the point estimate suggests a small positive association (0.24pp)
statistically inconclusive: primary p-value (0.060) exceeds 0.05
substantively small: absolute effect is ~0.24pp on a 1.2% baseline

given the burden of proof for a novel hypothesis, the weak and inconsistent evidence does not warrant concluding that referee bias by skin tone is established

experimental/quasi-experimental designs, objective skin tone measurement, detailed playing-style controls, and consistent cross-context effects would be needed to substantiate the hypothesis, but were not carried out here
